questions.q: Team A has probability $\frac{2}{3}$ of winning whenever it plays. Suppose A plays four games. What is the probability that A wins more than half of its games?

$\therefore \mathrm{p}=\frac{2}{3} \& \mathrm{q}=1-\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}$
Let $X$ denotes the number of winning games out of 4 games i.e. $n=4\therefore$ The probability of $r$ success 
$\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{r})={ }^{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{p}^{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{q}^{\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{r}}, \mathrm{r}=0,1,2,3,4\therefore$ Probability of winning more than half games $=\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X} \gt 2)=\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=3)+\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=4)=\binom{4}{3}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3} \cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{4-3}+\binom{4}{4}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{4} \cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{4-4}=\frac{4 !}{3 ! 1 !} \cdot \frac{8}{27} \cdot \frac{1}{3}+\frac{4 !}{4 ! 0 !} \cdot \frac{16}{81}=\frac{32}{81}+\frac{16}{81}=\frac{48}{81}=\frac{16}{27}$

If curver $=a \sin 3 \theta$ To trace the curve, we consider the following table : \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline 3 \theta= & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & \frac{3 \pi}{2} & 2 \pi & \frac{5 \pi}{2} & 3 \pi \\ \hline\theta= & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} & \frac{2 \pi}{3} & \frac{5 \pi}{6} & \pi \\ \hliner= & 0 & \mathrm{a} & 0 & -\mathrm{a} & 0 & \mathrm{a} & 0 \\ \hline \end{array} Thus there is a loop between $\theta=0 \& \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$ as r varies from $\mathrm{r}=0$ tor $=0$.
Hence, the area of the loop lying in the positive quadrant $=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} r^{2} \mathrm{~d} \theta=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin ^{2} \phi \cdot \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi$ [On putting, $\left.3 \theta=\phi \Rightarrow \mathrm{d} \theta=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi\right]=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{6} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin ^{2} \phi \mathrm{d} \phi=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{6} \cdot \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1-\cos 2 \phi}{2} \mathrm{~d} \phi\left[\because \cos 2 \theta=1-2 \sin ^{2} \theta\right]=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\phi+\frac{\sin 2 \phi}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+\sin \pi\right]=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2} \pi}{24}$

questions.q: Two point charges $4 \mu \mathrm{C}$ and $-2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ are separated by a distance of $1 \mathrm{~m}$ in air. Then the distance of the point on the line joining the charges, where the resultant electric field is zero, is (in metre)
questions.solution: Let the point $\mathrm{P}$ where resultant field is zero be $x \mathrm{~m}$ from $4 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge and $(1-\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{m}$ distance apart from $-2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ charge. Since field is zero at this point then, $\begin{array}{l} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{1}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{2}=0 \\ \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}|=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{\mathrm{q}_{1}}{\mathrm{r}_{1}^{2}}+\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{\mathrm{q}_{2}}{\mathrm{r}_{2}^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow 0=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}}\left[\frac{4 \mu \mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{x}^{2}}+\frac{(-2 \mu \mathrm{C})}{(1-\mathrm{x})^{2}}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \frac{4 \mu \mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{x}^{2}}=\frac{2 \mu \mathrm{C}}{(1-\mathrm{x})^{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{\mathrm{x}^{2}}=\frac{1}{(1-\mathrm{x})^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow 2(1-\mathrm{x})^{2}=\mathrm{x}^{2} \end{array} Taking root $\sqrt{2}(1-x)=x\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow 1.414(1-x)=x \Rightarrow 1.414-1.414 x=x \\ \Rightarrow 1.414=(1+1.414) x \Rightarrow x=\frac{1.414}{2.414} \\ \Rightarrow x=0.58 \mathrm{~m} \end{array}

questions.q: Figure shows a triangular array of three point charges. The electric potential $\mathrm{V}$ of these source charges at the midpoint $\mathrm{P}$ of the base of the triangle is $\left[\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}}=9 \times 10^{9} \mathrm{Nm}^{2} \mathrm{C}^{-2}\right]$
questions.solution:
The net electric potential is algebraic sum of potential due to individual point charges.
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{V} &=\frac{1}{4 \pi \in_{0}}\left[\frac{\mathrm{q}_{1}}{\mathrm{r}_{1}}+\frac{\mathrm{q}_{2}}{\mathrm{r}_{2}}+\frac{\mathrm{q}_{3}}{\mathrm{r}_{3}}\right] \\
\mathrm{V} &=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}\left[\frac{1 \times 10^{-6}}{0.2}-\frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.2}+\frac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.3}\right] \\
&=9 \times 10^{9}[5-10+10] \times 10^{-6} \\
&=9 \times 10^{3}[5]=45 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~V}=45 \mathrm{kV}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: In an experiment on Newton's rings, the diameter of the $20^{\text {th }}$ dark ring was found to be $5.82 \mathrm{~mm}$ and that of the $10^{\text {th }}$ ring $3.36 \mathrm{~mm}$. If the radius of the plano-convex lens is $1 \mathrm{~m}$, the wavelength of light used is
questions.solution:
Newton's ring arrangement is used for determining the wavelength of monochromatic light. For this the diameter of $n^{\text {th }}$ dark ring $\left(D_{n}\right)$ and $(n+p)^{\text {th }}$ dark ring $\left(\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{p}}\right)$ are measured then
$D_{(\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{p})}^{2}=4(\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{p}) \lambda \mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{n}}^{2}=4 \mathrm{n} \lambda \mathrm{R}\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{D_{n+p}^{2}-D_{n}^{2}}{4 p R}$
Here, $n=10, n+p=20\therefore \quad p=10 ; R=1 m, D_{10}=3.96 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}$,
$D_{20}=5.82 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}\therefore \lambda=\frac{D_{20}^{2}-D_{10}^{2}}{4 \mathrm{pR}}\quad=\frac{\left(5.82 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}-\left(3.36 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}}{4 \times 10 \times 1}\quad=5646 Å$
